findings.claim: Every lesson labels its practice questions '[20]' / '20 marks — Extract Analysis' and splits them into a part (a) extract task and a part (b) 'elsewhere in the play' task; seven exam tips, one conclusion, two knowledge checks and two flashcards repeat the 'Part (a) / Part (b)' format, and every mark scheme runs a 17–20 / 13–16 / 9–12 / 5–8 / 1–4 ladder.
findings.truth: The set-text drama question is ONE source-based question worth 40 marks with an extract printed on the paper. There is no part (a) or part (b) and no 20+20 split. Question stems relabelled to [40], types to '40 marks', and every band ladder rescaled to 33–40 / 25–32 / 17–24 / 9–16 / 1–8 to match the sibling Eduqas post-1914 units.
findings.evidence: specs/eduqas/english-literature-C720QS.md section 2.2 Component 2: Section A (20%) Post 1914 Prose/Drama, 40 marks, source based response, 'Section A assesses AO1, AO2 and AO4', closed book; paper is 2h30 for three 40-mark sections

findings.claim: The board is named in student-facing text: 'the Eduqas C720U Component 2 exam' (L1), 'In the Eduqas exam' (L1), 'the Eduqas Component 2 Section A question' (L1 exam tip), 'For the Eduqas exam' (L8 conclusion), 'What does AO2 assess in the Eduqas exam?' (L8 KC), 'What is the Eduqas Blood Brothers exam format?' (L8 flashcard).
findings.truth: House rule: Eduqas lessons never name the board or a spec code in student-facing text. Reworded to neutral phrasing ('the exam', 'your drama question').
findings.evidence: house rule in the checker brief; matches the fixes applied to english-literature-eduqas/a-taste-of-honey

findings.claim: Context is presented as earning marks: 'In the Eduqas exam, context must be embedded naturally' (L1 n14), 'context is not a separate paragraph — embed it into your analysis' (L1 exam tip), 'Context should be embedded naturally, not in a separate paragraph' (L8 n16), and L8 n14 hedges 'and, on some papers, AO4 (accuracy of written expression). Check your exam board’s specimen paper for the exact format and mark allocation.'
findings.truth: Section A assesses AO1, AO2 and AO4 only. AO3 (context) is NOT assessed on this question, so context earns no marks; AO4 (written accuracy) IS credited. The hedge about 'some papers' is replaced with the specification's fixed position.
findings.evidence: specs/eduqas/english-literature-C720QS.md section 2.2 Component 2: Section A (20%) Post 1914 Prose/Drama, 40 marks, source based response, 'Section A assesses AO1, AO2 and AO4', closed book; paper is 2h30 for three 40-mark sections

findings.claim: 'He confronts Eddie not as a rival but as a man who has lost everything: “You! You could have been me!”'
findings.truth: Mickey never says that. His words are 'You! You! Why didn’t you give me away mam? I could have been. I could have been him!' and they are addressed to Mrs Johnstone, not to Edward. The lesson reverses the pronouns and the addressee, and contradicts its own correct 'I could have been him!' two paragraphs later.
findings.evidence: LitCharts quote page (Mrs Johnstone & Mickey, Tell Me It's Not True) and the council-chamber quotation carried by knowunity and Scribd final-scene notes

findings.claim: 'At the Johnstones’ home, the policeman is aggressive and threatening: “I’ll be back, Mrs Johnstone. I’ll be back.” ... he calls Mr Lyons “sir,” laughs off the incident as “just a prank,” and shares a whisky.'
findings.truth: Fabricated quotation. The policeman tells Mrs Johnstone 'Either you keep them in order, missis, or it’ll be the courts for you, or worse, won’t it?' and tells Mr Lyons 'an’, er, as I say, it was more of a prank, really, Mr Lyons.' The 'sir' and the specific whisky are not attested; he does take a drink at the Lyons house.
findings.evidence: quotation banks quoting the policeman's two lines; LitCharts 'The Policemen' character page confirms the drink and the contrasting manner

findings.claim: '“They say that if either twin learns he was one of a pair, they shall both immediately die.”' (also in the L2 flashcard)
findings.truth: The line is 'if either twin learns that he once was a pair'. Russell's odd phrasing is the memorable part and students quote it.
findings.evidence: LitCharts, GradeSaver and knowunity quote banks all give 'he once was a pair' / 'he was once a pair'

findings.claim: 'Mickey is caught, and Sammy escapes. Mickey is sentenced to prison.'
findings.truth: Mickey freezes at the scene and is caught; Sammy runs but two policemen arrest him during the escape. Mickey's sentence is seven years.
findings.evidence: LitCharts Act 2 summary; Wikipedia plot summary (seven-year sentence)

findings.claim: 'He is the person who gives Mickey the gun.'
findings.truth: Sammy hides the gun under the floor at Mrs Johnstone's house before his arrest; Mickey retrieves it himself at the end. Lesson 5 states this correctly, so the unit contradicts itself.
findings.evidence: LitCharts 'Guns' symbol page and Act 2 summary; Wikipedia plot summary

findings.claim: 'the milkman and catalogue man come to repossess her belongings: “We’re not going to take them all, love. We’ll leave you one, you can swap each week.”' (repeated in the L1 practice stem and mark scheme)
findings.truth: The Catalogue Man and the Finance Man take the goods back; the Milkman's role is to refuse Mrs Johnstone further credit. The quotation is not attested in any source.
findings.evidence: LitCharts Act 1 summary (Catalogue Man and Finance Man remove her possessions); four searches found no such line

findings.claim: 'Unemployment trebled between 1979 and 1983, hitting 3.3 million.'
findings.truth: Unemployment was above 1.5 million in 1979 and about 3.2 million by June 1983 — slightly more than a doubling. The 3.3 million peak came in 1984.
findings.evidence: Hansard 1984 labour statistics debates; Wikipedia First/Second Thatcher ministry

findings.claim: 'The musical version of Blood Brothers premiered in London’s West End in 1983.'
findings.truth: It opened at the Liverpool Playhouse on 8 January 1983 and transferred to the Lyric Theatre in the West End on 11 April 1983. The premiere was in Liverpool, not London.
findings.evidence: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blood_Brothers_(musical)

findings.claim: 'Russell once said he wanted to write plays “for the people I grew up with, not the people who run the National Theatre.”'
findings.truth: No source attests this quotation. Replaced with the documented fact that Russell wrote the first version of the play for a Liverpool school company (Merseyside Young People's Theatre, Fazakerley Comprehensive, November 1981) rather than for a West End stage.
findings.evidence: two targeted searches of Russell interviews found nothing; Wikipedia for the 1981 school premiere

findings.claim: Linda 'can “throw stones better than any boy”' (also the L3 flashcard and the L6 knowledge-check answer key)
findings.truth: Not attested anywhere. What the play gives is Linda leading the mischief — she is the one who pushes the boys into throwing stones through windows. The claim is reworded so the knowledge-check answer 'stones' stays correct.
findings.evidence: GradeSaver 'Kid's Game' summary; Revision Genie Linda quote bank lists no such line

findings.claim: A section heading '“Take a Pill, Mickey”' and the claim that it 'becomes a refrain that echoes through the final act' (repeated in an L4 mark scheme)
findings.truth: No such line or refrain exists. The play runs the other way: Linda hides Mickey's pills and begs him to stop — 'I need you. I love you. But Mickey, not when you’ve got them inside you' — and he demands them back.
findings.evidence: LitCharts Act 2 summary; Revision Genie Linda quote bank

findings.claim: '“That Guy” ... The song is a soliloquy in musical form: Mickey cannot express these feelings in dialogue.'
findings.truth: 'That Guy' is a duet: Mickey and Edward each sing that they envy the other. Calling it a soliloquy misdescribes the form, which is exactly what AO2 credits on this question.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia musical-numbers list ('That Guy' – Mickey and Edward); LitCharts Act 2 summary

findings.claim: 'Mickey thinks Eddie’s vocabulary is hilarious — “you talk dead funny” — and is amazed that Eddie does not know the word “bogey.”'
findings.truth: The attested line is 'You sound dead funny swearin’ in that posh voice.' The 'bogey' claim is not attested; the real class-and-language gag is the dictionary — Edward says he will look the word up 'in the dictionary' and Mickey answers 'In the what?'
findings.evidence: quotation banks for the first-meeting scene; knowunity quote list (Edward: 'you say smashing things')

findings.claim: A mark scheme quotes the Narrator's opening as '‘Did you ever hear the story’ = storytelling convention.'
findings.truth: The opening line is 'So did y’ hear the story of the Johnstone twins?'
findings.evidence: LitCharts and GradeSaver quote pages (Narrator, Overture)

findings.claim: Flashcard: 'Which Mickey line captures the novel’s class argument?'
findings.truth: Blood Brothers is a play, not a novel. On a drama question this is the sort of slip that costs AO1 credibility.
findings.evidence: specification prescribes Blood Brothers as a post-1914 drama text

findings.claim: Mickey's line is given as '“I need them… they make me invisible.”'
findings.truth: Not verbatim, but the substance is right: Linda tells Mickey that when he takes the pills she cannot even see him, and Mickey says that is exactly why he takes them. Left alone rather than replaced with a paraphrase.
findings.evidence: LitCharts Act 2 summary; Seneca revision notes

findings.claim: Mickey's childhood gun cry '“I got y’! I shot y’!”' (repeated in L3, L5, L8) and the list of Mickey's Scouse ('Gis a sweet', 'youse', 'the bogey man').
findings.truth: Could not confirm this wording in any accessible source, and could not disprove it — Mickey's toy-gun play and 'Gis a sweet' are both attested. Left as written; worth a look if the play text ever reaches scripts/_retrofc/_texts/.
findings.evidence: LitCharts 'Guns' symbol page confirms the toy-gun games but not the wording

findings.claim: 'Mickey and Eddie first meet at the age of seven' and the knowledge check keyed to 'Seven'.
findings.truth: Correct as far as it goes: Edward gives his age as seven and Mickey answers 'I’m nearly eight.' What the lesson omits is the trigger for the pact — they find they share a birthday (18 July), which is why Mickey proposes they become blood brothers. Omission, not an error, so not edited.
findings.evidence: LitCharts quote page (MICKEY: What’s your birthday? / EDWARD: July the eighteenth. / MICKEY: So is mine.)

summary: All 8 lessons carried the same mark-affecting exam error: the unit teaches an invented two-part 20+20 question with a 17-20 band ladder, when the specification sets one source-based 40-mark question assessing AO1, AO2 and AO4 with an extract printed on the paper and no credit for context. On top of that: two fabricated quotations (the policeman's 'I'll be back' and Mickey's 'You could have been me'), a misquoted twin curse, an invented 'Take a pill, Mickey' refrain, Sammy wrongly escaping the robbery and wrongly handing Mickey the gun, and a Liverpool premiere reported as a West End one. 181 edits across all 8 lessons; the primary text is in copyright, so every quotation was checked against Wikipedia, LitCharts, GradeSaver and published quotation banks.
